title: When Mitigations Backfire: Timing Channel Attacks and Defense for PRAC-Based RowHammer Mitigations
problem: The JEDEC DDR5 Per Row Activation Counting (PRAC) mechanism and its Alert Back-Off (ABO) protocol and Refresh Management (RFM) commands introduce observable timing differences that create a new timing side-channel, allowing attackers to monitor memory access latencies and infer sensitive information such as cryptographic keys.
method: The paper first presents PRACLeak, a timing channel attack that exploits latency variations induced by ABO protocol and RFM commands to extract secret keys from vulnerable AES implementations by monitoring memory access timing. To counter this, the authors propose Timing-Safe PRAC (TPRAC), which replaces activity-triggered RFM commands with Timing-Based RFMs issued periodically and independently of memory activity, eliminating the observable correlation between memory access patterns and mitigation timing. TPRAC requires only a single-entry in-DRAM mitigation queue per bank and is designed to be compatible with existing DRAM standards.

title: Enterprise Class Modular Cache Hierarchy
problem: Enterprise mission-critical workloads demand cache hierarchies that deliver consistent low-latency performance at sustained processor utilization above 90% across diverse and highly virtualized workloads, while remaining extensible across processor generations and new technology insertions.
method: The IBM Telum and Telum II processors introduce a modular, horizontally federated cache hierarchy in which last-level cache slices are distributed across chiplets and interconnected through high-bandwidth on-chip links. An adaptive horizontal cache persistence algorithm dynamically adjusts which cache levels retain hot data across different access patterns and workload phases. The paper details how fetch events flow through this hierarchy and how cache size changes affect system-level performance, culminating in the Telum II design that simultaneously supports traditional enterprise workloads and generative AI inference.

title: FACIL: Flexible DRAM Address Mapping for SoC-PIM Cooperative On-device LLM Inference
problem: On-device LLM inference requires the same model weights to be accessed by both DRAM-based PIM units (for GEMV in the memory-bound decode phase) and SoC processors (for GEMM in the compute-bound prefill phase), but PIM-operable tensor layouts require different DRAM bank mappings from those preferred by SoC processors, creating costly re-layout overheads when switching between the two.
method: FACIL introduces a flexible DRAM address mapping scheme in the memory controller that assigns different DRAM address mappings to the page offset bits of each huge page. A user-level library determines the appropriate mapping for each tensor, allowing LLM weights to be placed in DRAM banks that are simultaneously PIM-operable and contiguously addressable by the SoC processor. This dual-mapping eliminates the need to copy or re-layout tensor data when switching between PIM-executed GEMV and SoC-executed GEMM operations.

title: QECC-Synth: A Layout Synthesizer for Quantum Error Correction Codes on Sparse Architectures
problem: Quantum Error Correction (QEC) codes require dense qubit connectivity that does not match the sparse qubit coupling graphs of current hardware architectures, and existing QEC circuit compilation approaches either underutilize QEC circuit structure or rely on manual, architecture-specific designs that do not generalize.
method: QECC-Synth is an automated compiler that uses the ancilla bridge technique—inserting ancilla qubits to implement long-range interactions over sparse coupling graphs—and systematically classifies the design space flexibilities of this technique. It then formulates the layout synthesis problem as a MaxSAT optimization problem over these flexibility dimensions, finding globally near-optimal ancilla placement and routing for a given QEC code and hardware architecture. This approach is architecture-agnostic and handles diverse QEC codes (e.g., surface code, color code) without manual redesign.

title: WindServe: Efficient Phase-Disaggregated LLM Serving with Stream-based Dynamic Scheduling
problem: Phase-disaggregated LLM serving systems that separate compute-bound prefill from memory-bandwidth-bound decoding still suffer from coarse-grained static scheduling that leaves prefill compute overloaded while decoding resources sit idle, creating queuing delays and underutilization. KV cache transfers between disaggregated phases introduce additional scheduling overhead that further degrades latency SLOs.
method: WindServe implements a global scheduler that continuously monitors compute and memory resource usage across prefill and decoding pools and dynamically orchestrates cross-phase job assignments to reduce queuing delay and KV-cache swapping overhead. A stall-free rescheduling strategy saturates memory resources while minimizing overhead from KV cache transfers between phases. A stream-based pipeline mitigates interference between prefill and decoding jobs running concurrently by separating their execution streams and managing dependencies asynchronously.

title: IntraFuzz: Coverage-Guided Intra-Enclave Fuzzing for Intel SGX Applications
problem: Intel SGX applications are vulnerable to intra-enclave software vulnerabilities; existing automated bug-finding methods focus on fuzzing enclave boundaries in simulated environments, missing vulnerabilities in actual hardware-protected enclaves.
method: IntraFuzz is the first system enabling efficient coverage-guided fuzzing of SGX applications inside actual hardware-protected Intel SGX enclaves. The system integrates with SGX runtime to instrument enclave code and collect coverage feedback during fuzzing, enabling hardware-based vulnerability detection on real SGX platforms.

title: An Algorithm-Hardware Co-design Based on Revised Microscaling Format Quantization for Accelerating Large Language Models
problem: Microscaling (MX) format offers promise as drop-in FP32 replacement but lacks practical hardware support; dominant low-precision LLM inference still relies on low-bit quantization, limiting scalability of MX format deployment.
method: Algorithm-hardware co-design with two levels: (1) RMFQ (Revised MX Format Quantization) introduces revised MX (RMX) format with novel group direction strategy for improved quantization; (2) RMFA (Revised MX Format Accelerator) implements RMX-adaptive hardware architecture and RMX encoding scheme optimized for low-bit operations.

title: Mosaic: Exploiting Instruction-Level Parallelism on Deep Learning Accelerators with iTex Tessellation
problem: Deep learning compilers use top-down tiling to map tensor computations homogeneously to a single type of hardware arithmetic unit (scalar, vector, or tensor), failing to exploit simultaneous use of all available compute units (scalar, vector, and tensor) in parallel. This leaves substantial instruction-level parallelism (ILP) on CPUs and GPUs unexploited, especially when computations can be decomposed into mixed instruction types.
method: Mosaic introduces iTex (instruction-level texture) tessellation: a compiler technique that decomposes a tensor computation task into heterogeneous sub-tiles assigned to different hardware arithmetic units (scalar, vector, tensor) simultaneously. The tessellation partitions the iteration space of a tensor operation such that different sub-regions are mapped to the most appropriate unit type, and the schedule coordinates their concurrent execution. A compiler pass analyzes operation shapes and hardware unit capabilities to determine the optimal tessellation, then generates mixed-instruction kernel code that overlaps scalar, vector, and tensor unit execution within a single kernel.

title: Late Breaking Results: Scalable GPU-Friendly Parallelization for Sweep-Based Maze Routing
problem: GPU-accelerated maze routing algorithms struggle with limited GPU memory resources on large-scale VLSI designs; sweep-based methods generate excessive kernel launching overhead.
method: Introduces sweep-sharing technique allowing multiple nets to be routed simultaneously within a single sweep process, substantially reducing memory consumption and kernel launching overhead. Proposes edge-level rip-up-and-reroute technique that selectively reroutes only overflowed segments while preserving feasible solution parts, reducing overall runtime.

title: AttenPIM: Accelerating LLM Attention with Dual-mode GEMV in Processing-in-Memory
problem: Attention computations in LLMs are memory-bound; PIM offloading ignores dynamic matrix dimensions (token-length-dependent) and distinct patterns between score ($Q \times K_t$) and context ($S \times V$) GEMVs, leading to inefficient uniform processing.
method: AttenPIM: dual-mode PIM computing tailored for score vs context computations; bank-level execution with configurable per-bank PIM units; PIM-oriented data layouts for KV storage; token-level and head-level concurrency for workload balance; dynamic allocation and kernel fusion.

title: Maximizing Energy Efficiency in Spiking Neural Networks: A Dynamic Joint Pruning Framework
problem: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) face energy and computational efficiency challenges due to growing architectural complexity, requiring aggressive pruning that balances multiple sparsity dimensions simultaneously.
method: A dynamic joint pruning framework combines multi-stage masking for fine-grained neuron firing threshold control, temporal attention batch normalization (TABN) with learnable time scaling, and a dynamic sparse strategy that adjusts importance coefficients based on real-time SOP (synaptic operation) computational impact.

title: Fair-CO2: Fair Attribution for Cloud Carbon Emissions
problem: Existing cloud carbon attribution methods unfairly allocate operational and embodied carbon footprints to tenant workloads by ignoring dynamic demand effects on embodied carbon amortization and interference effects in colocated scenarios. This leads to mispriced carbon signals that fail to incentivize workload-level carbon optimization.
method: Fair-CO2 adopts the Shapley value from cooperative game theory as a theoretically fair ground truth for shared-cost attribution, capturing both dynamic demand effects on embodied carbon (hardware amortized proportionally to actual utilization, not flat time allocation) and interference effects from workload colocation. Because exact Shapley computation scales exponentially with the number of workloads, Fair-CO2 approximates it via two tractable components: demand-aware embodied carbon attribution (adjusting hardware depreciation by real-time utilization) and interference-aware resource cost attribution (accounting for performance degradation from co-tenancy). Monte Carlo simulations over workload schedules and colocation scenarios are used to validate the approximation's fidelity to the exact Shapley solution.

title: DiTile-DGNN: An Efficient Accelerator for Distributed Dynamic Graph Neural Network Inference
problem: Dynamic Graph Neural Networks (DGNNs) combine GNN and RNN computations over evolving graph snapshots, creating combinatorial challenges of heterogeneous operator types, intra- and inter-snapshot data dependencies, redundant data across snapshots, and load imbalance that prevent efficient parallel scaling.
method: DiTile-DGNN uses a redundancy-free parallelism framework that analytically identifies snapshot-level data overlap and eliminates redundant computation while minimizing inter-node communication complexity. A workload-balance optimizer removes synchronization barriers between snapshots. A reconfigurable accelerator architecture with flexible interconnect dynamically adapts to support multiple DGNN dataflows (GNN aggregation, RNN recurrence, and their combination) without hardware redesign.

title: BitMoD: Bit-serial Mixture-of-Datatype LLM Acceleration
problem: LLM deployment is constrained by large weight memory footprints; existing low-precision quantization schemes either sacrifice too much accuracy or lack hardware support for multiple heterogeneous data types simultaneously. Current accelerators cannot efficiently process mixed numerical formats (e.g., INT4, FP4, NF4) within a single design.
method: BitMoD is an algorithm-hardware co-design that introduces fine-grained per-group (128-weight) data-type adaptation, selecting from a set of carefully designed numerical types to minimize quantization error per group. On the hardware side, a bit-serial processing element natively handles multiple precisions by decomposing weights into bit-planes; a unified representation maps all data types to a common internal format, and a dedicated bit-serial dequantization unit rescales per-group partial sums with minimal overhead.

title: Accelerating LLM Serving for Multi-turn Dialogues with Efficient Resource Management
problem: Current LLM serving frameworks recompute attention keys and values for all prior turns on each new query in a multi-turn dialogue, incurring substantial redundant compute overhead. Additionally, the long accumulated prompt lengths from multi-turn context cause head-of-line blocking under FCFS scheduling, underutilizing GPU resources.
method: The paper introduces efficient resource management for multi-turn LLM serving by preserving KV-cache state across turns to eliminate recomputation of prior-turn attention keys and values. A new scheduling policy replaces FCFS with a length-aware or priority-based scheduler that avoids head-of-line blocking by reordering or preempting long-prompt requests. KV-cache memory is managed dynamically to balance cache retention across concurrent multi-turn sessions, trading off memory capacity against recompute cost.

title: LAD: Efficient Accelerator for Generative Inference of LLM with Locality Aware Decoding
problem: In LLM autoregressive decoding, the KV cache grows linearly with sequence length, and at lengths beyond 2048 tokens the attention mechanism's repeated read of the full KV cache becomes the dominant bottleneck, consuming over 50% of total inference time on GPU-based systems.
method: LAD (Locality Aware Decoding) is a dedicated ASIC accelerator that exploits numerical locality in attention scores across consecutive decoding steps. The key insight is that when an attention score at a specific sequence position remains approximately constant across several consecutive decoding steps, the corresponding key and value vectors need not be re-fetched at every step. LAD implements a locality detection engine that identifies stable-score positions and caches their contribution, dramatically reducing KV cache access frequency while maintaining decoding accuracy. The hardware includes specialized attention decoding units paired with on-chip score history buffers to track and exploit inter-step score locality.
